edition.locus: Vossius 1684 Opera omnia (archive bub_gb_DY2xvRwPetMC), Latin column, Duodecim Capita de Fide, Cap. XI, printed pp. 5-6 (PDF pp. 29-30)

source_text: Si quis dicit corpus Christi esse inanimatum, aut sine mente; et non confitetur ipsum perfectum esse hominem per omnia unum et eundem; anathema esto. Qua ratione potest ullus dicere, corpus Christi esse sine anima, aut mente? Turbatio enim, et dolor, et pavor, neque carnis sunt inanimatae, nec animae non intelligentis; neque divinitatis immutabilis; nec ostensio inanis apparitionis; neque infirmitatis humanae succumbentis defectus: sed passiones naturae nostrae in seipso Verbum ostendebat, suscipiens partem ad patiendum datam. Sicut scriptum est: Quoniam ipse infirmitates nostras assumpsit, et languores nostros ipse tulit. Turbatio enim, et dolor, et pavor, languores animae sunt: defatigatio autem, et somnus, et vulneratio corporis, infirmitates carnis sunt.
thought_title: Christ's body was not without soul or mind
orientation: Gregory condemns the view that Christ's body had no soul or mind, and shows that his distress, grief and fear belong to a human soul.
pass_a_gloss: If anyone says the body (corpus) of Christ to be soulless (inanimatum), or without mind (sine mente); and does not confess him to be a perfect man (perfectum hominem) in all things one and the same (unum et eundem); let him be anathema. By what reason can anyone say the body of Christ to be without soul (anima) or mind? For disturbance (turbatio), and grief (dolor), and fear (pavor) are neither of soulless flesh, nor of a soul not understanding (non intelligentis); nor of unchangeable divinity (divinitatis immutabilis); nor a display (ostensio) of empty appearance (inanis apparitionis); nor a failing (defectus) of human weakness (infirmitatis) succumbing (succumbentis): but the Word was showing (ostendebat) in himself the passions (passiones) of our nature (naturae), taking up (suscipiens) the part given for suffering (ad patiendum). As it is written: That he himself assumed (assumpsit) our weaknesses (infirmitates), and bore (tulit) our ailments (languores). For disturbance, and grief, and fear are ailments of the soul: but weariness (defatigatio), and sleep (somnus), and wounding (vulneratio) of the body are weaknesses of the flesh.

pass_b_english: If anyone says that the body of Christ is soulless or without mind, and does not confess that he is a perfect man, in all things one and the same, let him be anathema.

How can anyone say that the body of Christ is without soul or mind? For distress, grief and fear belong neither to flesh without a soul, nor to a soul without understanding, nor to the unchangeable divinity. Nor are they the show of an empty appearance, nor the failure of a human weakness that gives way. Rather, the Word was displaying in himself the passions of our nature, taking up the part that was given over to suffering. As it is written, “He himself took up our weaknesses and bore our ailments” (Isaiah 53:4; Matthew 8:17). For distress, grief and fear are ailments of the soul; but weariness, sleep and the wounding of the body are weaknesses of the flesh.
notes: Inanimatum rendered “soulless”; mens “mind” and intelligens “understanding”, against the view that Christ had no human soul or no human mind.
Turbatio rendered “distress” (being troubled, as in John 12:27).
Languores and infirmitates are kept apart as “ailments” and “weaknesses” because the closing sentence assigns the first to the soul and the second to the flesh.
The quotation blends Matthew 8:17 (ipse infirmitates nostras accepit) with Isaiah 53:4 (languores nostros ipse tulit); margin siglum Esai. 53.
Quoniam before the quotation is a mark of quotation and is not translated.
The anathema begins at the foot of printed p. 5 and ends on p. 6; no reading problem.
